newsitem.title: ALBANIA: OSCE envoy says West must support Albania with aid.
newsitem.headline: OSCE envoy says West must support Albania with aid.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky, welcoming Albania's election as a vital first step towards normality in the chaotic Balkan republic, said on Tuesday the international community must now follow through with economic support.

Vranitzky, who brokered a deal between Albania's squabbling political parties in March to hold the early election, had brief meetings with President Sali Berisha and interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino soon after arriving in Tirana on Tuesday.
The former Austrian chancellor said he was told by Berisha that he had accepted the verdict of the people which meant his Democratic Party would now be entering opposition.

Asked whether Berisha said he would step down after five years in power, Vranitzky replied: "No, he did not mention it and I did not ask him." Diplomatic sources said Berisha look tired and glum during the meeting with Vranitzky.

"The election that took place on Sunday and the election that has still to take place on July 6 are to be considered as a first step...towards reconstructing Albania," Vranitzky told reporters after meeting the president.
Rebuilding the shattered economy, modernising infrastructure and reforming the judiciary and other institutions had to be the top priorities when financial support from the West began, he said.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) all had a role in injecting new financial blood into the former communist state.
"It has to be made quite clear that once the elections are over...that everyone in the international community is not going to pack their suitcases and go home," Vranitzky said.

Fino's Socialist Party has claimed a resounding victory in the first round of the general election, called just 13 months after a nationwide votel widely regarded by foreign observers as seriously tainted.
Berisha's Democrats won most seats in parliament in the 1996 election while the Socialists and other rival parties boycotted the vote.

Albania's Central Electoral Commission has yet to announce any official results from Sunday's election but Berisha made a televised address to the nation on Monday to concede defeat in a statement many Albanians understood to be a hint that he was stepping down.
As head of state, Berisha has to wait for parliament to be convened before he can offer his resignation, analysts said.
Vranitzky said Fino had told him a government was likely to be formed by the end of July.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which had more than 500 international observers monitoring the vote, declared in a preliminary report that the voting process was "adequate and acceptable".

Vranitzky and OSCE election certification officer Catherine Lalumiere were to leave Tirana on Tuesday evening for Copenhagen to brief the OSCE's chairman-in-office, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen.
"I will suggest in Copenhagen to set up a working group... to come up with a number of ideas so that Albania can be supported in the future," Vranitzky said.
No one has yet suggested how law and order can be restored in Albania's south, where armed gangs hold sway in the wake of unrest sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes.
Sunday's election process and the generally peaceful voting was praised by several European states.
John Shattuck, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Democracy and Human Rights, and 50 American observers also monitored Sunday's elections and concurred with the findings of the OSCE.
The delegation said the counting of votes, though contentious, fell "within the boundaries of overall international standards".

The Vienna-based International Helsinki Federation, which also sent monitors to Albania, said the election reflected the will of the people but urged the incoming government to improve the country's human rights record.
